The same source generates celbridge-tokens.css, the token sheet served to WebView content, so a color declared here holds the same value inside a web panel. Each color names its web counterpart alongside it. The WinUI control keys redirected onto this palette are emitted here too, once per theme, because a brush declared over the theme dictionaries would answer to the operating system's theme rather than the element's.
cssHeader: Celbridge design tokens, served at /assets/celbridge-client/celbridge-tokens.css. Generated from Source/Core/Celbridge.DesignTokens/DesignTokens.json. Do not edit this file: edit the token source and rebuild.

This is the tokens-only sheet: the --cel-* custom properties and nothing else. Link it directly when an editor wants the host's colors and fonts but brings its own chrome and does not want the bare-element control styling in celbridge.css (the CodeEditor is the precedent, its toolbar and Monaco surface are styled by hand and should not inherit generic button/input rules). Utilities that want the full package link celbridge.css instead, which imports this file and adds the base and control layers on top.

The same source generates the native app's theme dictionaries, so a color declared here holds the same value in the host chrome. Theme follows html[data-theme], which the client mirrors from the host on every state snapshot (see core/state-store.js). The accent color is the application's own rather than the one the operating system supplies, so it holds the same value in a web panel as it does in the chrome. The monospace font is the bundled Cascadia Mono, imported below. The UI font is a system stack, matching the host chrome per platform.

font-ui.value: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI Variable Text", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

groups.comment: The type scale, mirroring the named TextBlock styles in Celbridge.UserInterface/Resources/Styles.xaml. Keep the two in sync when either changes. Small carries panel titles, field labels and supporting prose. Base carries input, button and body text. Heading carries the section heading.

radius-button.comment: Rounding on a flat icon button, mirroring the IconButtonCornerRadius resource in Celbridge.UserInterface/Resources/Styles.xaml. Keep the two in sync when either changes. A step beyond the control radius, which a button carrying no border reads better at.

comment: The scale the web engine applied on top of the host's own rasterization scale, mirrored from the host on every state snapshot (see core/state-store.js). On Windows it carries the accessibility text scale, which the engine folds into its rasterization scale rather than treating as a text setting, so a CSS pixel here is larger than a device-independent pixel in the native chrome. 1 where the two agree, which is every platform without that setting.

A dimension that has to line up with the native chrome divides by it, so that declaring it smaller and rendering it at engine scale lands on the native value. The type sizes deliberately do not: text already matches, because both stacks grow it by the same factor.

groups.comment: Icon and control sizing, mirroring the standardized values in Celbridge.UserInterface/Resources/Styles.xaml. Keep the two in sync when either changes.

Vertical icon rail sizing, mirroring the workspace utility rail (WorkspaceConstants.UtilityPanelRailWidth, which sizes the panel's rail column, and UtilityButton.xaml's cell and button). The column carries the whole band up to the panel beside it, with no gutter between the two, so the square button centred in a square cell is what holds the channel open. Keep the three in sync when any changes.
Title strip above a panel's content, mirroring the native PanelHeader (PanelHeader.xaml). Keep the two in sync when either changes.
Inset from a panel's edge to its content, mirroring the ScrollViewer padding the native settings panels use (PackagesSectionView.xaml). Keep the two in sync when either changes.

Grab band of a splitter dividing two panes of one document, mirroring the GrabAreaSize set on the native Splitter where it does the same job (WebViewDocumentView.xaml). Console.js carries a third copy for its drag arithmetic. Keep the three in sync when any changes. Wider than the 7px workspace gutter because a band inside a document has no field behind it to widen the target.

comment: The smallest size at which a document is legible. Every minimum in the workspace layout is composed upward from this one pair, so the space the host reserves for a document never falls below it, and a document laying itself out against these values works to the same floor the host does.
Mirrored by WorkspaceConstants.DocumentMinWidth and DocumentMinHeight, which the native composition reads. Keep the two in sync when either changes.

Two background roles. Content is a canvas a document is edited or viewed in. Chrome is the surface everything else sits on, including the channels between panels. A region painted with content is carved out of the chrome surface and outlined with the panel edge.

The panel edge draws every line that bounds something: a carved region, a card, a splitter band. The divider draws a rule between two bands inside one of those. Both are chosen for legibility against the surface behind them rather than to rank one above the other.

content-background.darkComment: Content sits within four units of the Monaco and terminal canvases, so a document's own chrome meets its canvas without a visible seam.

divider.comment: A fraction lighter than the edge. On a light surface the edge tone reads heavy for an internal rule. On a dark one it does not, so the two match there.

divider-subtle.comment: The subtle translucent divider (WinUI DividerBrush), used for hairline rules within a surface.

accent.comment: The accent is the application's own, not the one the operating system supplies. It carries meaning here, marking the selected category or the primary action, so it is held at a known contrast against the surfaces and the text drawn over it rather than left to a setting outside the application.
accent.darkComment: A mid blue rather than a light one, so the same white sits over it as on the light theme. The cost is prominence: against the chrome surface it reads at about three to one, where a light accent reads at nearly eight.

accent-hover.comment: The accent under the pointer, for the web surfaces. It darkens on both themes, which is the direction that protects the white over it. The native side has no counterpart because WinUI derives its own hover from the accent ramp.

accent-pressed.comment: A second step along the hover direction, so a press reads as further travel rather than a different colour.

accent-text.comment: Whatever is drawn over an accent fill. One value rather than a pair: both accents are dark enough to carry white, which is what choosing a mid blue on the dark theme buys. WinUI holds a fixed black-on-dark, white-on-light pair for text over its own accent fills, so anything left on its default reads black where ours read white. The accent button is redirected here because its style resolves AccentButtonForeground and the hover and press variants by key. Its disabled state is left alone, having no tone in this palette. What stays out of reach is a style binding TextOnAccentFillColorPrimaryBrush itself, which WinUI reaches through a StaticResource alias captured at parse time.

text-secondary.comment: Mirrors WinUI TextFillColorSecondary (#9E000000 light, #C5FFFFFF dark), so a web panel's secondary text matches the native panels beside it.

error-text.comment: The counterpart to warning-text at the next severity up, drawn from the same palette so the two read as one scale.

caution.comment: Attention pip fill (WinUI SystemFillColorCaution), matching the pips on the native rail and tab strip.

selection-background.comment: The wash over anything selected, whether that is a row in a list or a run of text. Translucent so it reads over whichever surface it lands on, and built from the accent of its own theme, so a selection and a focus ring are the same blue.

groups.comment: Control fill, hover, and border, approximating WinUI's ControlFillColorDefault and ControlStrokeColorDefault system brushes. There is no XAML counterpart, because native controls take those system brushes directly. Shared by buttons and form inputs.

control-background.darkComment: Stepped off the content background, which an editor's body takes, by the same amount a control used to step off chrome, so a control on a content surface reads no more inflated than it did before.

groups.comment: The states a flat button takes under the pointer, wherever it sits: the utility rail, the application toolbar, a panel toolbar. One pair rather than one per surface, so every flat button in the application reads the same. Chosen to carry against both chrome and the content canvas, which the WinUI list tones do not: they land within a few units of a light surface and leave the hover invisible there.

button-hover-background.darkComment: A wider step off chrome than the light theme takes. The same numeric distance separates two dark tones far less than two light ones, and at the light pair's step a hover over chrome is barely there.

button-active-background.comment: A surface that is on screen while its panel is unfocused. A step beyond hover, so a button already showing its surface still reads as the selected one under the pointer.

groups.comment: Card fills. The header holds the same tone as a control fill, since both are a raised surface sitting one step off the content canvas. The content fill is chosen against it rather than inherited from WinUI, whose value leaves every boundary in an expanded card near-invisible.
